parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 3. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning her new neighbour to ask about gyms in the area. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. David: Hello? Anna: Hi, David, it's Anna from number fourteen. We met on Saturday when I was moving in. David: Oh, hi, Anna. Are you settling in all right? Anna: Yes, thanks. I hope you don't mind me calling, but you mentioned you knew a lot about the gyms round here. I'd really like to join one, but there seem to be so many. David: No problem at all. Well, the biggest one is FitZone, on the High Street. I've been a member there for about three years. It's about five minutes' walk from here, so it's very convenient. Anna: What does it cost? David: They've got different types of membership. The cheapest is twenty-five pounds a month, and that goes up to thirty-nine pounds a month if you want to use everything, including the sauna. Anna: Right. And is it good? David: It is. The building itself is quite old, but the equipment is all very new. They replaced everything last year. And at the moment they've got a special offer. If you join before the end of the month, you get a free towel. It gets very busy between six and eight in the evening, though, so I usually go early in the morning. Anna: A towel? That's not very exciting. David: No, but it's better than nothing. Last year it was a free session with a personal trainer, which was much more useful. Anna: What are the opening hours like? David: It's open from six in the morning until ten at night, every day except Christmas. Anna: Hmm. It sounds a bit expensive for me, to be honest. Is there anywhere else? David: There's Kirby Leisure, out near the ring road. You'd need to drive or get the bus, but there's a big car park. Anna: Sorry, what was that? David: Kirby. K, I, R, B, Y. It's mid-priced, I'd say. But be careful, because they charge an extra ten per cent a month if you want to go to any of the classes, like yoga or spinning. Anna: Oh, I'd definitely want to do some classes. David: Well, they're worth it, apparently. And they've got a crèche, if that's any use. Anna: Not for me, but it's good to know. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. David: Then there's the Riverside Club. It's the cheapest place in town, both for using the gym and for the swimming facilities. The pool's really good, actually. The changing rooms are a bit old-fashioned, but the staff are very friendly. Anna: That sounds perfect. I love swimming. David: A couple of things to bear in mind, though. They provide towels, but they don't give you anything to lock your things away with, so you'll need to bring your own padlock for the lockers. Anna: That's easy enough. David: And you have to sign up for at least twelve months. There's no monthly option. Anna: Hmm, I'm not sure I want to commit for that long. I'm only on a one-year contract at work, and I might move again after that. David: That's understandable. A lot of people feel the same way. David: Oh, and I've just remembered one more. It's quite new. It's called The Forge, like a blacksmith's forge. It's in that old factory building by the station. A friend of mine goes there and says it's got a really good atmosphere, lots of young people. Anna: What are their prices like? David: I'm not sure, and I think they've been changing them quite a lot. They have an app, but the prices on it aren't always up to date, so it's best to look at their website. Anna: OK, I'll do that. David: The good thing about The Forge is that new members can have a free trial for a week, so you can see if you like it before you pay anything. Anna: That's a great idea. I think I'll try there first. Thanks so much, David, that's really helpful. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking to a group of visitors at a restored walled garden. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Grace: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashcombe Walled Garden. My name's Grace, and I coordinate the volunteers who look after the garden. Before you explore, I'd like to tell you a little about its history and about the work that's gone into it. Grace: The garden was built in the eighteen-fifties to supply fruit, vegetables and flowers to Ashcombe House, which you can see through the trees. But by the nineteen-seventies it was no longer needed, and it was simply abandoned. For forty years, it was completely overgrown. Grace: People often assume that the family who own the house, or perhaps the county council, were behind the restoration. In fact, it was a group of people from the village who first had the idea. They set up a charitable trust in 2012, and persuaded the owners to lease them the land. The council did give us a small grant later on, but the initiative came from local residents. Grace: One of our first problems was that we had no idea what the garden had originally looked like. We hoped there would be plans at the house, but they'd been lost in a fire. We also spoke to a man whose grandfather had worked here as a gardener, but he didn't remember very much. Then, by pure chance, one of our volunteers found an album of old photographs in an antique shop, taken in about 1905, which showed almost every part of the garden. That's what we've based everything on. Grace: Clearing the site took two whole summers. There were brambles everywhere, and dozens of trees had grown up inside the walls, which was hard work. But the most difficult job by far was repairing the walls themselves. Some sections had collapsed completely, and we had to have bricks specially made to match the originals. Grace: You might expect our volunteers to be mostly retired gardeners, and we do have a few of those. But in fact, they come from every background you can imagine: students, office workers, parents with young children, even a couple of teenagers doing it for a school award. Grace: People often ask what happens to everything we grow. For the first few years, we sold vegetables in the shop, but now almost all of it goes to the food bank in town, which helps families who are struggling. The café, by the way, buys its ingredients from a farm nearby, because we simply can't grow enough. Grace: And as for the future, we've considered opening in the evenings during the summer, but it isn't really practical. What we're going to do instead is run gardening courses for local schools, starting next spring. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Grace: Now, if you look at your map, you'll see we're standing at the main gate, at the bottom. There are a few things I'd particularly recommend you see. Grace: As soon as you come through the gate, look to your right. In the corner there, against the wall, you'll find the fountain. It had been completely buried under soil, and we only discovered it when we started clearing that area. Grace: The shop is on the left as you come in, near the gate, but please don't go there yet. It's much better to visit at the end. Grace: The building we're proudest of is the glasshouse. To get there, follow the main path straight ahead, past the sundial in the centre, and keep going until you've almost reached the far wall. The glasshouse is on the right-hand side of the path. It's full of peaches and grapes at this time of year. Grace: The herb garden is also worth a visit. It's right up in the far left-hand corner of the garden, so it's the furthest point from where we are now. It was originally used to grow herbs for medicines as well as for cooking. Grace: And finally, don't miss the tool museum. When you get to the sundial, turn right along the cross path, and walk to the very end. The museum is right against the wall there, at the end of the path. It has hundreds of old gardening tools that were found on the site. Grace: Right, that's enough from me. Please enjoy your visit. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two design history students, Lily and Omar, discussing their project on the history of postcards. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Lily: So, Omar, I've finished my part of the research on postcards. How's yours going? Omar: Not bad. I was surprised how hard it was to find good sources online. Most websites are just people selling old cards. But I'm really glad we chose this topic. Nobody else in the group is doing anything similar, even though our tutor wrote a book about it. Lily: That might be exactly why nobody else chose it. They'd be worried about getting something wrong. Omar: Maybe. Or they just didn't think postcards sounded very exciting. Lily: Well, they're wrong. I've found it fascinating. I had no idea how much you could learn from them. Omar: True. Anyway, I found out that a lot of people believe picture postcards were invented by the Post Office. Lily: Yes, I came across that too. But it's not right. In Britain, the Post Office only produced plain cards at first, with a printed stamp and no picture. The pictures came from private publishers, once they were allowed to print their own cards. Omar: What surprised me was a rule about the early picture cards. The back was only for the address, so you had to squeeze your message onto the front, around the picture. Lily: I know. Some people wrote across the sky in the photograph. It wasn't until 1902 that you could put the message on the back. And a lot of people wrote so small that you can hardly read it now without a magnifying glass. Omar: I'd already read that there were several postal deliveries a day in cities then, so people could send a card in the morning to arrange to meet someone the same afternoon. Lily: That's something I think we should explain properly, actually: why so many cards were sent in the early nineteen-hundreds. Millions every week. It was cheap and quick, the nearest thing they had to sending a text message. People sent them for all sorts of reasons: to say they'd arrived safely, to wish someone happy birthday, or just to say hello. Omar: Definitely. We should also compare the early cards with the later ones. Lily: The cards from the nineteen-fifties and sixties are much more colourful, of course, and there's a lot more variety in the designs. Some of them use really bright, almost unnatural colours. Omar: But I actually prefer the early ones, because the messages tell you so much about ordinary life: the weather, what people ate, who was ill. Lily: I agree. As historical sources, they're far more informative. Omar: And what about after the Second World War? Lily: Well, there was a shortage of paper for a few years, which is understandable. What I don't really get is why the designs hardly changed at all for about twenty years afterwards. Every seaside card looked exactly the same. Omar: It is strange. Lily: Maybe publishers just kept using the same photographs because it was cheaper. I'll try to find out. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Lily: I've picked out some cards we could use in the presentation. This first one's a view of a harbour. Omar: It's hand-coloured, isn't it? The detail is amazing. It could almost be a painting in a gallery. Lily: That's what I thought. What about yours, Omar? I'd love to use it on the title slide. Omar: I've got a card that a soldier sent home from France in 1916. I chose it because of the message. He describes what it's like living in the trenches, and tries to reassure his mother that he's fine. Lily: That's really moving. Then there's this one, of a parliament building on the day it first opened. It was printed to celebrate the country becoming independent, so it marks a key moment in the nation's history. Omar: Great. And the last one is from the city archive. It's one of the first cards they put online when they began digitising their collection last year. They've already scanned about fifty thousand. Lily: I wish I'd known about that before I started. It would have saved me hours in the library. Anyway, shall we start putting the slides together this afternoon? Omar: Good idea. I'm free after two. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear an architecture lecturer talking about biophilic design. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about an approach to architecture that has become very influential over the past twenty years: biophilic design. The word biophilia literally means love of life, and the idea behind it is that human beings have an inborn need to feel connected with nature. Biophilic design, then, is about creating buildings and spaces that strengthen that connection, so that the people who use them feel healthier and happier. The term was made popular by the biologist Edward O. Wilson in the nineteen-eighties, although architects only began to take it seriously much later. Lecturer: It's sometimes confused with green design, but the two are not quite the same. Green design is mainly concerned with the building's effect on the environment: reducing emissions, using less water, choosing sustainable materials. Biophilic design focuses instead on the effect of the building on the people inside it. Of course, many buildings try to do both. In fact, the best examples combine the two, so that a building is both good for the planet and good for the people who spend their days in it. Lecturer: So what does biophilic design look like in practice? The most obvious feature is the use of living plants. In many new offices, you'll see whole walls covered in plants, sometimes several storeys high. Natural light is also important, so designers try to make sure that as many people as possible can see the sky from where they work. Where that isn't possible, some offices use screens or lighting that imitates the changing colour of daylight during the day. Lecturer: Materials matter too. Wood is widely used in place of plastic and metal, because people respond to its natural patterns and textures, even when they're not consciously aware of it. And it isn't only about what we see. Some buildings play quiet recordings of birdsong in corridors and waiting areas. It may sound strange, but studies suggest it can make people feel calmer. Lecturer: What's the evidence that any of this actually works? One of the most famous studies was carried out in a hospital in the United States in the nineteen-eighties. It compared patients recovering from the same operation. Those whose rooms had a view of trees recovered faster and needed fewer painkillers than those whose windows faced a brick wall. The results were so striking that they encouraged hospitals around the world to rethink the design of their wards. Lecturer: Since then, there have been many studies of workplaces. Employees in offices with natural elements often report feeling less stressed, and several studies have found improvements in their creativity. The evidence for higher productivity is more mixed, although companies naturally hope for that too. Staff turnover also tends to be lower in such buildings, which saves employers money. Lecturer: Schools are another area where biophilic design is being tried. In some classrooms that have been redesigned with more daylight and plants, teachers report that children's concentration has improved, although it's hard to separate this from other changes that were made at the same time. Lecturer: Now, biophilic design is not without its critics. One practical issue is cost. Not so much the cost of installation, which is often lower than people expect, but the fact that living walls and indoor gardens need regular maintenance. If plants aren't properly looked after, they quickly die, and a wall of dead plants is worse than no plants at all. Lecturer: Another problem is health. Most people benefit from being around plants, but for some, particularly those who suffer from allergies, certain species can cause real problems, so designers need to choose them carefully. There's also a concern that some companies simply add a few plants for the sake of their image, without really thinking about the needs of the people who work there. Lecturer: In the second half of today's lecture, I'm going to look at some examples of buildings where these ideas have been put into practice, starting with a hospital in Singapore. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer coordinator talking to a group of visitors at a restored walled garden. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 16. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 16. Grace: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Ashcombe Walled Garden. My name's Grace, and I coordinate the volunteers who look after the garden. Before you explore, I'd like to tell you a little about its history and about the work that's gone into it. Grace: The garden was built in the eighteen-fifties to supply fruit, vegetables and flowers to Ashcombe House, which you can see through the trees. But by the nineteen-seventies it was no longer needed, and it was simply abandoned. For forty years, it was completely overgrown. Grace: People often assume that the family who own the house, or perhaps the county council, were behind the restoration. In fact, it was a group of people from the village who first had the idea. They set up a charitable trust in 2012, and persuaded the owners to lease them the land. The council did give us a small grant later on, but the initiative came from local residents. Grace: One of our first problems was that we had no idea what the garden had originally looked like. We hoped there would be plans at the house, but they'd been lost in a fire. We also spoke to a man whose grandfather had worked here as a gardener, but he didn't remember very much. Then, by pure chance, one of our volunteers found an album of old photographs in an antique shop, taken in about 1905, which showed almost every part of the garden. That's what we've based everything on. Grace: Clearing the site took two whole summers. There were brambles everywhere, and dozens of trees had grown up inside the walls, which was hard work. But the most difficult job by far was repairing the walls themselves. Some sections had collapsed completely, and we had to have bricks specially made to match the originals. Grace: You might expect our volunteers to be mostly retired gardeners, and we do have a few of those. But in fact, they come from every background you can imagine: students, office workers, parents with young children, even a couple of teenagers doing it for a school award. Grace: People often ask what happens to everything we grow. For the first few years, we sold vegetables in the shop, but now almost all of it goes to the food bank in town, which helps families who are struggling. The café, by the way, buys its ingredients from a farm nearby, because we simply can't grow enough. Grace: And as for the future, we've considered opening in the evenings during the summer, but it isn't really practical. What we're going to do instead is run gardening courses for local schools, starting next spring. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 17 to 20. Grace: Now, if you look at your map, you'll see we're standing at the main gate, at the bottom. There are a few things I'd particularly recommend you see. Grace: As soon as you come through the gate, look to your right. In the corner there, against the wall, you'll find the fountain. It had been completely buried under soil, and we only discovered it when we started clearing that area. Grace: The shop is on the left as you come in, near the gate, but please don't go there yet. It's much better to visit at the end. Grace: The building we're proudest of is the glasshouse. To get there, follow the main path straight ahead, past the sundial in the centre, and keep going until you've almost reached the far wall. The glasshouse is on the right-hand side of the path. It's full of peaches and grapes at this time of year. Grace: The herb garden is also worth a visit. It's right up in the far left-hand corner of the garden, so it's the furthest point from where we are now. It was originally used to grow herbs for medicines as well as for cooking. Grace: And finally, don't miss the tool museum. When you get to the sundial, turn right along the cross path, and walk to the very end. The museum is right against the wall there, at the end of the path. It has hundreds of old gardening tools that were found on the site. Grace: Right, that's enough from me. Please enjoy your visit. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two design history students, Lily and Omar, discussing their project on the history of postcards. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26. Lily: So, Omar, I've finished my part of the research on postcards. How's yours going? Omar: Not bad. I was surprised how hard it was to find good sources online. Most websites are just people selling old cards. But I'm really glad we chose this topic. Nobody else in the group is doing anything similar, even though our tutor wrote a book about it. Lily: That might be exactly why nobody else chose it. They'd be worried about getting something wrong. Omar: Maybe. Or they just didn't think postcards sounded very exciting. Lily: Well, they're wrong. I've found it fascinating. I had no idea how much you could learn from them. Omar: True. Anyway, I found out that a lot of people believe picture postcards were invented by the Post Office. Lily: Yes, I came across that too. But it's not right. In Britain, the Post Office only produced plain cards at first, with a printed stamp and no picture. The pictures came from private publishers, once they were allowed to print their own cards. Omar: What surprised me was a rule about the early picture cards. The back was only for the address, so you had to squeeze your message onto the front, around the picture. Lily: I know. Some people wrote across the sky in the photograph. It wasn't until 1902 that you could put the message on the back. And a lot of people wrote so small that you can hardly read it now without a magnifying glass. Omar: I'd already read that there were several postal deliveries a day in cities then, so people could send a card in the morning to arrange to meet someone the same afternoon. Lily: That's something I think we should explain properly, actually: why so many cards were sent in the early nineteen-hundreds. Millions every week. It was cheap and quick, the nearest thing they had to sending a text message. People sent them for all sorts of reasons: to say they'd arrived safely, to wish someone happy birthday, or just to say hello. Omar: Definitely. We should also compare the early cards with the later ones. Lily: The cards from the nineteen-fifties and sixties are much more colourful, of course, and there's a lot more variety in the designs. Some of them use really bright, almost unnatural colours. Omar: But I actually prefer the early ones, because the messages tell you so much about ordinary life: the weather, what people ate, who was ill. Lily: I agree. As historical sources, they're far more informative. Omar: And what about after the Second World War? Lily: Well, there was a shortage of paper for a few years, which is understandable. What I don't really get is why the designs hardly changed at all for about twenty years afterwards. Every seaside card looked exactly the same. Omar: It is strange. Lily: Maybe publishers just kept using the same photographs because it was cheaper. I'll try to find out. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30. Lily: I've picked out some cards we could use in the presentation. This first one's a view of a harbour. Omar: It's hand-coloured, isn't it? The detail is amazing. It could almost be a painting in a gallery. Lily: That's what I thought. What about yours, Omar? I'd love to use it on the title slide. Omar: I've got a card that a soldier sent home from France in 1916. I chose it because of the message. He describes what it's like living in the trenches, and tries to reassure his mother that he's fine. Lily: That's really moving. Then there's this one, of a parliament building on the day it first opened. It was printed to celebrate the country becoming independent, so it marks a key moment in the nation's history. Omar: Great. And the last one is from the city archive. It's one of the first cards they put online when they began digitising their collection last year. They've already scanned about fifty thousand. Lily: I wish I'd known about that before I started. It would have saved me hours in the library. Anyway, shall we start putting the slides together this afternoon? Omar: Good idea. I'm free after two. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear an architecture lecturer talking about biophilic design. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about an approach to architecture that has become very influential over the past twenty years: biophilic design. The word biophilia literally means love of life, and the idea behind it is that human beings have an inborn need to feel connected with nature. Biophilic design, then, is about creating buildings and spaces that strengthen that connection, so that the people who use them feel healthier and happier. The term was made popular by the biologist Edward O. Wilson in the nineteen-eighties, although architects only began to take it seriously much later. Lecturer: It's sometimes confused with green design, but the two are not quite the same. Green design is mainly concerned with the building's effect on the environment: reducing emissions, using less water, choosing sustainable materials. Biophilic design focuses instead on the effect of the building on the people inside it. Of course, many buildings try to do both. In fact, the best examples combine the two, so that a building is both good for the planet and good for the people who spend their days in it. Lecturer: So what does biophilic design look like in practice? The most obvious feature is the use of living plants. In many new offices, you'll see whole walls covered in plants, sometimes several storeys high. Natural light is also important, so designers try to make sure that as many people as possible can see the sky from where they work. Where that isn't possible, some offices use screens or lighting that imitates the changing colour of daylight during the day. Lecturer: Materials matter too. Wood is widely used in place of plastic and metal, because people respond to its natural patterns and textures, even when they're not consciously aware of it. And it isn't only about what we see. Some buildings play quiet recordings of birdsong in corridors and waiting areas. It may sound strange, but studies suggest it can make people feel calmer. Lecturer: What's the evidence that any of this actually works? One of the most famous studies was carried out in a hospital in the United States in the nineteen-eighties. It compared patients recovering from the same operation. Those whose rooms had a view of trees recovered faster and needed fewer painkillers than those whose windows faced a brick wall. The results were so striking that they encouraged hospitals around the world to rethink the design of their wards. Lecturer: Since then, there have been many studies of workplaces. Employees in offices with natural elements often report feeling less stressed, and several studies have found improvements in their creativity. The evidence for higher productivity is more mixed, although companies naturally hope for that too. Staff turnover also tends to be lower in such buildings, which saves employers money. Lecturer: Schools are another area where biophilic design is being tried. In some classrooms that have been redesigned with more daylight and plants, teachers report that children's concentration has improved, although it's hard to separate this from other changes that were made at the same time. Lecturer: Now, biophilic design is not without its critics. One practical issue is cost. Not so much the cost of installation, which is often lower than people expect, but the fact that living walls and indoor gardens need regular maintenance. If plants aren't properly looked after, they quickly die, and a wall of dead plants is worse than no plants at all. Lecturer: Another problem is health. Most people benefit from being around plants, but for some, particularly those who suffer from allergies, certain species can cause real problems, so designers need to choose them carefully. There's also a concern that some companies simply add a few plants for the sake of their image, without really thinking about the needs of the people who work there. Lecturer: In the second half of today's lecture, I'm going to look at some examples of buildings where these ideas have been put into practice, starting with a hospital in Singapore. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
